Chapter 6: Knowing Your BATNA — Strengthening Your Negotiation Power
Let’s dive into something that can really change the way you negotiate—knowing your BATNA. Now, BATNA stands for Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement. Think of it like your backup plan, your safety net. When you’re clear about your BATNA, you walk into any negotiation with confidence, knowing you won’t settle for less than you deserve.
Picture yourself shopping for a used car. If you know there’s another car out there, at a fair price, you’re not going to feel pressured to accept a bad deal from the first seller you meet. That’s your BATNA in action—it gives you real leverage, because you can always walk away if the terms just aren’t right.
So, how do you actually build and use your BATNA? Here’s a simple process you can follow:
First, make a list of every alternative you have if this deal falls through. What could you do instead? Next, look at each of those alternatives closely. How valuable are they? Are they truly realistic? After that, pick the one that stands out as your best option—that’s your BATNA.
But don’t stop there. Try to estimate what the other side’s BATNA might be, too. If you know their options, you’ll be able to fine-tune your strategy and spot where you have an edge.
Let’s make this real with a job negotiation example. Maybe your BATNA is another job offer, sticking with your current position, or even going freelance. The stronger your alternatives, the more power you bring to the table. And if your alternatives are a bit weak? That’s a sign you might want to strengthen them before sitting down to negotiate.
Here’s something to keep in mind—your BATNA isn’t a tool for threats. It’s your private yardstick, helping you decide what’s actually good for you. It keeps you from saying yes to a deal that’s worse than just walking away.
When both sides know their BATNAs, the whole conversation becomes more grounded. Everyone’s aware of their boundaries, and that makes it easier to focus on solutions that are truly better than the alternatives. You’re less likely to accept a bad deal just because you’re nervous or feeling desperate.
So, if you want to negotiate with real confidence, always know your BATNA—and use it as your anchor.
